newsitem.title: USA: The boss's open door means more time for employees.
newsitem.headline: The boss's open door means more time for employees.

text.p: When retailer Mercantile Stores exchanged its midtown Manhattan headquarters in 1990 for a converted warehouse in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield, Ohio, CEO David Nichols thought a central office would give him a better handle on operations.

"He wanted to have a pulse on the organisation, and they (employees) likewise on him, so he's in an office with three clear glass walls supported by black steel ribbing, a totally open entrance, and no doors, relatively in the centre of the building," said Steve Schlegel, vice president of Hixson Architecture Engineering & Interiors, Cincinnati, which converted the 266,000-square-foot warehouse.
Nichols "wanted to create a new culture," said Schlegel, one in which employees could "interreact without any roadblocks."

"He always wanted open, easy access so that people could feel they could come right in," said Rosemary Uliano, Nichols' executive secretary. "Our conference rooms are all glass with glass doors, too, so you could walk by and see who was in there and you could call them out and they can call you in," she added.
When he stands at his desk, Nichols can survey rows of chest-high partitions in the taupe-hued interior where many of the 1,000 headquarters staffers work.
In Mercantile's old New York headquarters, corporate executives were bunched together.
"The 'adjacency approach' is still important, who is close to whom, and that won't go away," Schlegel said, "but it's not enough to design an office around adjacencies."

"Everyone is on one level now," said Bernard Breitenbach, public relations director for the merchandiser, which has annual sales of $2.9 billion, "whereas in New York there were five floors we had to use, which took departments and teams away from one another."
Future office design, Schlegel believes, will be centred around "knowledge distribution," driven by:
-- technology, or computers, software, and communications;
-- "the company's work processes, culture and micro-cultures;"
-- and gaining "competitive advantage through people."

"Companies that create a physical environment that enables their employees to feel better about their work and provide the tools for them to work faster and smarter, will outperform those that don't," affirms Jeffrey Pfeffer, organisational behaviourist at the Stanford Graduate School of Business. "It's surprising, but many of today's managers ignore this fact."
Yet many managers do pay attention.

"It's standard design procedure now to create flexible work stations oriented to the computer terminal with adequate file storage and work surface," said Ted Halsey, a project designer with Anderson Mason Dale, a Denver architectural firm.

"The partitions provide privacy when seated and visibility when standing. This way there's control of audible conversations but yet there is eye contact when you need to see somebody. It's not like you have to knock on their door," Halsey said.
Using cross-functional teams, Schlegel said, means "you change from the concept of everybody works in silos to working concurrently together," with space for their unique technologies.

"Most organisations have given space to people based on who they are. With teamwork, you give space to people based on what they do. That's why the walls are coming down," said Rick Mohr, manager of advanced solutions for Steelcase, the Grand Rapids, Mich., office furniture maker.
He sees a trend toward smaller, individual offices which, when supplemented with "a team space, a reading space, and a social space, you may come out ahead."

A survey of 150 "Fortune 1000" executives conducted this Spring for Hixson by Worthlin Worldwide, of Washington, D.C., found that three in four of them "would give up their private offices if they knew it would enhance their companies' productivity."
"Senior executives take a bad rap and often are accused of being out of touch with their employees," Schlegel said. "The results of this survey suggests the barrier is not attitudinal, but physical."

While the majority of those polled reject the idea that most of their employees will be largely telecommuting, sharing space, or "hoteling" in the near future, most say by year 2000 one in five of their employees will be working without a designated desk or office space.
Driving this change, Schlegel said, is that 83 percent of the executives said their firms "are working in teams or going towards working in teams."
The survey "confirms our belief that an office facility has to do much more than keep the rain off people," Schlegel added.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
